title: Su'ad Has Gone
intro: Ka'b ibn Zuhayr made this poem after the Prophet had declared his life forfeit for satirising him. Ibn Ishaq tells how, with nowhere left to turn, he composed it, set out for Medina and stayed with a man of Juhayna, who brought him to the Prophet at the dawn prayer; Ka'b prayed with him, then sat before him, put his hand in his and asked for safety, and Ibn Hisham reports that he recited the poem in the mosque. It opens, as the old odes do, with a love passage on Su'ad and her fickleness, moves through a long description of a she-camel that could carry him to her, then to the slanderers and the friends who abandoned him, and ends with his plea to the Prophet, praise of him, and praise of the emigrants of Quraysh. Al-Zirikli records that the Prophet pardoned him and gave him his own mantle (burda), and that the poem has drawn many commentaries, expansions and imitations.

translation: Su'ad has gone, and my heart today is sick with love,
enslaved in her wake, a captive in chains, unransomed.
1.sharh: The poem opens, as old Arabic odes do, with the departed beloved. Whether Su'ad was a real woman, perhaps his wife, or only the conventional name of the opening is not known.

translation: And Su'ad, the morning they set off and parted,
was a soft-voiced fawn, eyes lowered, dark-lidded.
2.sharh: The beloved is a young gazelle: a nasal softness in its cry, languid eyes, lids dark as if with kohl.

translation: Slim-waisted coming towards you, full-hipped going away;
no one could say she was too short or too tall.
3.sharh: Seen coming and going, her figure meets the old ideal both ways.

translation: When she smiles she shows teeth bright with moisture,
as if they had been given wine to drink, and again.
4.sharh: Her mouth is fresh and sweet, as if wine had been poured on it twice.

translation: Wine cut with cold water from a bend in a valley,
clear, in a pebbled bed, chilled by the north wind at mid-morning.
5.sharh: The comparison keeps unfolding: the water mixed into the wine is itself described, pure, cold and fanned by the north wind.

translation: The winds blow the specks off it, and it brims
with the rain of a night cloud, white bubbles rising.
6.sharh: Every detail adds to the purity of the water, and so to the freshness of her mouth, which is what all of this describes.

translation: Oh, what a friend she would be, if only she kept
her promises, or would listen to advice.
7.sharh: He admires her and pities her in one breath: she has every quality but faithfulness.

translation: But she is a friend in whose very blood are mixed
hurt, and lies, and broken promises, and change.
8.sharh: Her faults are in her nature, mixed into her blood; she cannot help them.

translation: She never stays as she is for long,
but shifts like a ghoul changing her robes.
9.sharh: She is as unstable as the ghoul, and as dangerous to follow.

translation: She holds to the pledge she claimed to give
no better than sieves hold water.
10.sharh: The proverbial sieve: water poured into it runs straight out.

translation: Don't be fooled by the hopes she raised and her promises:
hopes and dreams only lead astray.
11.sharh: He talks to himself, as the old poets often did.

translation: The promises of Urqub are her model,
and her promises are nothing but lies.
12.sharh: Urqub's name was a byword for promises never kept.

translation: I hope and long for her love to come near,
though I don't think you will give me anything.
13.sharh: Hope survives everything. The turn from “her” to “you” brings her suddenly close.

translation: Su'ad is now in a land that only
the finest, fleetest, easy-paced camels can reach,
14.sharh: Her distance opens the long description of a she-camel, a set piece of the old ode, which runs to line 34.

translation: and none will take me there but a strong, great she-camel
that keeps her quick pace even when tired,
15.sharh: Two kinds of fast gait are named; the second likens her to a mule.

translation: one whose sweat streams from behind her ears,
bent on roads whose waymarks are erased, unknown.
16.sharh: Sweat behind the ears was the sign of a good camel. Her task is the trackless desert.

translation: She scans the unseen road with a lone white wild bull's eyes
when the stony ground and the sand ridges blaze.
17.sharh: The wild bull, alone in the desert, was thought the sharpest-eyed of animals.

translation: Thick where the collar goes, full where the hobble goes,
built better than the stallion's other daughters.
18.sharh: A thick neck and full legs mean strength for the road.

translation: Thick-necked, hard-cheeked, solid, built like a male,
broad in the flank, long in front.
19.sharh: A pile of epithets, each a quality a rider looked for; “long in front” means a long neck, or a long stride.

translation: Her hide, like a sea turtle's, is not dented
by a starved tick on the sunny side of her back.
20.sharh: Her hide is so tough that not even a tick can bite into it.

translation: Lean and hard; her brother is her father, of noble stock,
her uncle her mother's brother; long-necked, swift.
21.sharh: The riddle means her line is pure: her sire covered his own mother, so her father is also her brother, and his half-brother is both her uncle on the father's side and on the mother's.

translation: A tick walks on her, then slips off
her breast and her flanks, so smooth they are.
22.sharh: Her coat is too sleek for a tick to hold on.

translation: Sturdy as a wild ass, packed with flesh on every side,
her elbows twisted out clear of her ribs.
23.sharh: Elbows that stand clear of the chest let a camel stride without chafing, the mark of a good mount.

translation: As if what juts beyond her eyes and throat,
her muzzle and her jaws, were a long hard stone.
24.sharh: Her long, hard face is likened to a stone.

translation: She goes by with a tail like a bare palm stalk, tufted,
over an udder no milking has drained.
25.sharh: She is not milked, so she keeps her strength for the road.

translation: Hook-nosed; in her ears, to an eye that knows,
plain signs of breeding, and her cheeks are smooth.
26.sharh: A connoisseur reads her pedigree in her ears.

translation: She races on light legs, keeping up with the fastest,
lean legs that barely touch the ground.
27.sharh: Her feet touch the ground no more than an oath is fulfilled by a token act: lightly, and only just.

translation: Brown-sinewed, they leave the pebbles scattered;
no shoes protect them from the stony hilltops.
28.sharh: Her legs are hard enough to need no protection.

translation: As if the swing of her forelegs, when she sweats
and the mirage has wrapped the hillocks,
29.sharh: A long simile begins here and lands in line 32.

translation: on a day when the chameleon stands scorched,
its sunward side as if roasted in hot ashes,
30.sharh: The chameleon, which turns to face the sun, is the poets' sign of a blazing day.

translation: when the drover tells his men, as the dark crickets
start kicking at the pebbles, “Stop for the midday rest,”
31.sharh: Even the crickets hop on the burning stones, and the caravan must halt.

translation: in the noon heat, were a tall woman's arms in her prime,
risen to mourn, answered by bereaved women,
32.sharh: The simile lands: the camel's forelegs flail like the arms of a woman beating her breast in mourning.

translation: wailing, her upper arms gone slack; she has
no wits left since the heralds told of her firstborn's death.
33.sharh: The mourner's frenzy is painted in full, as the old odes liked to do with their similes.

translation: She tears at her breast with her hands, and her shift
is ripped to rags down from her collarbones.
34.sharh: The commentators see a further likeness: grief has made her numb to pain, as the camel is numb to fatigue.

translation: The slanderers swarm about her, and what they say
is, “Son of Abi Sulma, you are a dead man.”
35.sharh: Here the poem turns from the journey to his danger: the Prophet had declared his life forfeit. Some read “about her” as about Su'ad.

translation: And every friend I had counted on said,
“Don't come looking to me: I have my own troubles.”
36.sharh: In his danger, his friends desert him.

translation: I said, “Get out of my way, curse you:
whatever the Merciful has decreed will be done.”
37.sharh: He meets their desertion with resignation to fate.

translation: Every son of woman, however long he stays safe,
will one day be carried on a hunched frame.
38.sharh: The hunched frame is the bier: since death comes to all, no one should gloat over his.

translation: I have been told that God's Messenger has threatened me,
and forgiveness is hoped for from God's Messenger.
39.sharh: The plea begins: the threat is real, but so is the hope of pardon.

translation: Go gently, may He guide you who gave you the gift
of the Quran, full of counsel and plain explanation.
40.sharh: He speaks to the Prophet directly. The Quran is a gift over and above prophethood.

translation: Do not take me by what the slanderers say, for I
have done no wrong, however much is said of me.
41.sharh: He blames his danger on the slanderers rather than on his own verses.

translation: I stand where I see and hear things
that, if the elephant stood there and heard them,
42.sharh: He is standing before the Prophet; the sentence runs on into the next line.

translation: it would stand trembling, unless
the Messenger, by God's leave, granted it safety.
43.sharh: The elephant, the largest of beasts, would shake in the presence he stands in.

translation: I kept cutting across the desert, wearing
the dark like armour, night's robe let down,
44.sharh: He recalls the night journey that brought him to Medina.

translation: until I placed my right hand, offering no resistance,
in the hand of one who punishes, whose word is final.
45.sharh: Putting one's right hand in another's was the gesture of submission and allegiance.

translation: He is more awesome to me, as I speak to him,
with “You will be held to account and questioned” in my ears,
46.sharh: The comparison runs on: the Prophet is more fearsome than the lion of the next lines.

translation: than a lion, the fiercest of lions, whose lair is
in the hollow of Aththar, thicket behind thicket,
47.sharh: Aththar, a valley famous for its lions, guards a lair hidden deep in dense growth.

translation: who goes out at dawn to feed two cubs whose food
is the flesh of men, dragged in the dust, torn apart.
48.sharh: The lion's portrait grows more terrible line by line.

translation: When he leaps on an equal, he will not
let him go until he is broken.
49.sharh: He fights only those worthy of him, and never loses.

translation: Because of him the beasts of the valley stay hushed,
and no bands of men go walking through his valley.
50.sharh: Fear of him silences every other creature.

translation: And in his valley there is always some brave man
eaten, his weapons and his rags strewn about.
51.sharh: Only the bravest dare his valley, and they do not come back.

translation: The Messenger is a sword that gives light to see by,
a blade of Indian steel, one of God's swords, drawn.
52.sharh: Both readings, “sword” and “light”, are old. The sword fits a custom the commentators recall: flashing a blade so that people far off could find their way to it.

translation: among young men of Quraysh, one of whom said,
in the valley of Mecca when they embraced Islam, “Leave!”
53.sharh: He turns to the emigrants who left Mecca for Medina.

translation: They left, and those who left were no weaklings, none who break
in battle, none who slip in the saddle, none unarmed.
54.sharh: Every kind of coward is named, and denied.

translation: High-nosed heroes, whose clothing in battle
is mail of David's weaving.
55.sharh: Pride and honour, and armour worthy of a prophet's make.

translation: Bright long coats, their rings driven through one another,
like the round pods of the qaf'a, tightly woven.
56.sharh: The links of their mail are likened to the ring-shaped pods of a desert plant.

translation: They walk like stately white camels, guarded
by their sword-strokes when the short dark men turn and run.
57.sharh: Ibn Ishaq reports that the Ansar of Medina took “the short dark men” as a gibe at them, since one of them had asked to kill Ka'b; Ka'b later made amends in a poem praising them.

translation: They do not exult when their spears strike
an enemy, nor despair when they are struck.
58.sharh: Victory is nothing new to them, and loss does not shake them.

translation: Spears strike them only in the chest,
and they never hang back from the pools of death.
59.sharh: Wounds in front mean they never turn their backs.

1.1.5.meaning: Matbul: struck down by love, sick with it.

2.2.2.meaning: Aghann: a young gazelle with a nasal note in its cry.

7.2.4-5.head: لَو أَنَّ
7.2.4-5.meaning: Law-anna, “if”: the hamza is dropped and its vowel moved back, as the metre needs.

9.2.5.head: الغول
9.2.5.meaning: Ghul: a desert demon that took one shape after another to lead travellers astray.

12.1.3.head: عُرقوب
12.1.3.meaning: Urqub: a man proverbial for broken promises; he kept putting off a friend's share of a palm's dates until he had harvested them himself by night.

17.1.4.head: مُفرَد
17.1.4.meaning: Mufrad: a lone wild bull, the oryx, thought the keenest-eyed of beasts.

20.1.3.head: أَطوم
20.1.3.meaning: Atum: a thick-skinned sea turtle; some say the giraffe.

21.1.1.meaning: Harf: a lean, hard she-camel, likened to a mountain ledge.

30.1.4.head: الحِرباء
30.1.4.meaning: Hirba': the chameleon, which turns to face the sun.

35.2.3-5.head: اِبن أَبي سُلمى
35.2.3-5.meaning: “Son of Abi Sulma”: the poet himself; Abu Sulma was his grandfather, the father of Zuhayr.

36.2.2.head: أَلفى
36.2.2.meaning: “Let me not find you”: don't come to me. The Sira and Jamharat ash'ar al-Arab have “let me not distract you”.

37.1.4-6.head: لا أَبا لَكُم
37.1.4-6.meaning: La aba lakum, “may you have no father”: an exclamation of contempt or impatience.

40.1.5.head: نافِلَة
40.1.5.meaning: Nafila: a gift beyond what is due; the Quran, a gift over and above prophethood.

44.2.5.meaning: Masdul: let down, hanging loose. The Sira has masbul, with the same sense.

45.2.4.head: نَقِمات
45.2.4.meaning: “Of punishments”: one who takes vengeance on his enemies.

47.2.2.meaning: Aththar: a valley near Tabala, famous for its lions.

52.1.3.head: سَيف
52.1.3.meaning: Sayf, “sword”: the Sira and Jamharat ash'ar al-Arab have nur, “a light”.

53.1.2.head: فِتيَة
53.1.2.meaning: Fitya: young men, generous ones. The Sira and Jamharat ash'ar al-Arab have usba, “a band”.

55.2.3.meaning: David, the prophet, credited in the Quran with making coats of mail.

56.2.3.head: القَفعاء
56.2.3.meaning: Qaf'a: a desert plant whose round pods look like the rings of mail.

57.2.5.head: التَّنابيل
57.2.5.meaning: Tanabil: short men; as a taunt, cowards.

59.2.4-5.head: حِياض المَوت
59.2.4-5.meaning: “The pools of death”: where death is met, the battlefield.
